metadata.title: The impact of teacher deep collaboration on job satisfaction: Evidence from Chinese lower secondary teachers

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data with a stratified two-stage probability sampling design (schools selected first, then ~20 teachers per school). The analytic sample is restricted to Shanghai, China, and includes 3,976 junior high school teachers from 198 schools. The manuscript does not report applying TALIS sampling weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the analysis is conducted via multilevel structural equation modeling in Mplus using robust maximum likelihood (MLR). Because the paper does not specify weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate design variables, readers should treat the estimates as model-based associations within the Shanghai sample rather than fully design-weighted population estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study models latent constructs and relationships among TALIS questionnaire scales (e.g., teacher deep collaboration, team innovation, self-efficacy, job satisfaction) using multilevel structural equation modeling rather than cognitive achievement scores with plausible values. As a result, plausible values are not part of the analysis pipeline. The manuscript also does not describe a missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation, or FIML) for questionnaire items, so the missing-data handling is a reporting gap that limits assessment of potential bias from item nonresponse.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data restricted to the Shanghai, China (CSH) sample of junior high school teachers. The analytic sample comprises 3,976 junior high school teachers from 198 schools. The paper reports demographic missing counts for some background variables (e.g., gender missing = 1; educational attainment missing = 13; career stage missing = 23) but does not specify an explicit exclusion rule for missing questionnaire items beyond the reported final N.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) Junior high school teachers
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel SEM (MSEM/MLC-MSEM, Mplus 8.3, MLR). Direct effect: TDC → TJS β = 0.087, SE = 0.018, Z = 4.75, p < 0.001. Model fit: SRMRwithin = 0.002, SRMRbetween = 0.03, AIC = 66080.889, BIC = 66225.496. Explained variance at teacher level: R2 = [0.046, 0.098].
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) junior high school teacher the study leveraged teacher deep collaboration to predict teacher job satisfaction, finding that teacher deep collaboration had a significant positive direct effect (β = 0.087, p < 0.001). This indicates that strengthening deep, feedback-oriented teacher collaboration may improve teachers’ job satisfaction, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) Junior high school teachers
main_findings.performance_metrics: Direct effect: TDC → TI β = 0.214, SE = 0.021, Z = 10.303, p < 0.001.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) junior high school teacher the study leveraged teacher deep collaboration to predict team innovation, finding that teacher deep collaboration significantly increased team innovation (β = 0.214, p < 0.001). This indicates that policies and school practices that promote sustained team-based collaboration with instructional feedback may foster teachers’ innovation-oriented mindsets and behaviors.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) Junior high school teachers
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) junior high school teacher the study leveraged teacher deep collaboration and team innovation to predict teacher self-efficacy, finding that both predictors had significant positive effects (TDC → TSE β = 0.196, p < 0.001; TI → TSE β = 0.199, p < 0.001). This indicates that deep collaboration can build teachers’ confidence in engaging students and using instructional strategies, suggesting that collaboration initiatives may work partly by strengthening efficacy beliefs.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) Junior high school teachers
main_findings.performance_metrics: Partial mediation: TDC → TI → TJS β = 0.054, SE = 0.007, Z = 7.689, p < 0.001 (MP = 29.2%); TDC → TSE → TJS β = 0.026, SE = 0.004, Z = 5.846, p < 0.001 (MP = 14.3%). Chain mediation: TDC → TI → TSE → TJS β = 0.006, SE = 0.001, Z = 5.449, p < 0.001 (MP = 3.1%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, China) junior high school teacher the study leveraged teacher deep collaboration to predict teacher job satisfaction through mediation by team innovation and teacher self-efficacy, finding significant indirect effects for both pathways (TDC → TI → TJS β = 0.054, p < 0.001; TDC → TSE → TJS β = 0.026, p < 0.001) and a smaller sequential chain effect (β = 0.006, p < 0.001). This indicates that collaboration initiatives may improve job satisfaction partly by increasing innovation and efficacy beliefs, though the sequential pathway appears modest and causality cannot be established from cross-sectional data.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data restricted to Shanghai, China, covering 3,976 junior high school teachers from 198 schools. It tests a multilevel structural equation modeling framework (Mplus 8.3, robust maximum likelihood MLR) to estimate direct and indirect relationships among teacher deep collaboration (T3COLES), team innovation (T3TEAM), teacher self-efficacy (T3SEENG), and teacher job satisfaction (T3JOBSA). The model fit is strong (SRMRwithin = 0.002; SRMRbetween = 0.03), and teacher deep collaboration shows a significant positive direct effect on job satisfaction (β = 0.087, p < 0.001). Mediation results indicate partial indirect effects via team innovation (β = 0.054, p < 0.001; MP = 29.2%) and via self-efficacy (β = 0.026, p < 0.001; MP = 14.3%), with a smaller chain effect (β = 0.006, p < 0.001; MP = 3.1%). Limitations include cross-sectional data (no causal inference) and no reported missing-data handling strategy.
